title: Stateful dependency fallback proxy and degradation playbook
creator: Riya Shah
description: Design and implement a lightweight stateful fallback proxy plus an operational playbook to improve availability when downstream Redis/Kafka/DB dependencies are degraded or unavailable. The proxy sits in front of existing dependency clients and provides: connection pooling and per-tenant soft quotas, short-lived local caches with bounded staleness for reads, write degradation modes (queue-to-disk / async buffer) and controlled circuit-breaker mechanics to prevent resource exhaustion during partial outage or regional failover.
background_and_motivation: We see recurring incidents where transient downstream overloads (Redis thundering, DB failovers, Kafka broker saturation) cause cascading request queues at the runtime layer. Existing connection pools either exhaust sockets (causing OS-level failures) or block request threads, increasing tail latency and SLO violations. A small, focused proxy that can (1) shed load gracefully, (2) return degraded but acceptable responses for reads, (3) queue writes for later retry, and (4) surface clear metrics and signals for SLO-driven routing will reduce customer-impacting outages.
proposed_solution_summary:
Implement 'dep-proxy' as a sidecar process for each region/service group. Key behaviors:
- Per-backend circuit breakers (error-rate and latency windows) with three states: closed, open, half-open. Open -> reject or degrade immediately.
- Local LRU cache for Redis GETs and idempotent DB reads with configurable TTL and max-staleness header.
- Write buffering for non-critical mutations: durable append-to-local-queue, backpressure to callers when queue is saturated.
- Connection leasing model: per-tenant soft limit + global pool trim policy with tokenized leases and jittered reclamation to avoid synchronized drops.
- Multi-region failover hooks: when regional broker is unhealthy, proxy will attempt cross-region read fallback (with marker) and route writes to an async replication pipeline.
slo_definitions:
Target SLOs for downstream interactions (applies to calls passing through dep-proxy):
- Redis reads (GET): p95 < 8ms, p99 < 25ms, error-rate < 0.1% per 5m window.
- Redis writes (SET/INCR): p95 < 12ms, p99 < 50ms, error-rate < 0.5% per 5m.
- Kafka produce: p95 < 50ms, p99 < 200ms, publish error-rate < 0.5%.
- DB reads (read-replica): p95 < 30ms, p99 < 120ms, error-rate < 0.2%.
If downstream violates these SLOs for >2 consecutive 1m windows, proxy escalates circuit-breaker and triggers degraded behavior.
circuit_breaker_policy:
Implementation details:
- Windowing: 1m sliding window for latency and 1m window for error-rate.
- Thresholds: error-rate > 5% OR p95 latency > configured threshold => open breaker for 60s.
- Progressive open: first open duration = 60s, exponential backoff up to 15m if repeated failures.
- Half-open probe: allow 5% of traffic through as canary; if success for 30s, close.
- Fast path: for non-critical reads, when open => serve from local cache (if present) and add response header 'X-Dep-Proxy-Degraded: true'.
- For writes: when open => enqueue to local durable queue and respond with 202 Accepted (where caller semantics allow). If queue full => respond 503 with guidance header 'Retry-After'.
connection_pooling_model:
Goals: avoid file-descriptor exhaustion, prevent head-of-line blocking, and isolate noisy tenants.
- Global pool size per node is capped (configurable by instance type).
- Per-tenant soft quotas: tenants have a borrow token budget; tokens are consumed on lease, returned after idle timeout.
- Admission control: when tenant exceeds soft quota, proxy applies one of: (a) slow-path queuing with tokenized priority, (b) denial with 429, (c) tenant-specific shedding profile.
- Eviction policy: least-recently-used plus tenant-priority watermark; trim gradually with randomized jitter to avoid mass reconnects.
degradation_modes:
Ordered list of degradation strategies (applied progressively):
1) Prefer local cache misses filled asynchronously; return stale read with TTL annotation.
2) Switch reads to read-replica or cross-region mirror (with lower consistency guarantee).
3) Convert synchronous writes to async buffered writes (202 accepted) if client supports eventual durability.
4) If buffers saturate, apply tenant-scoped rate limits and return 429/503 with explicit reason codes.
5) If region completely unavailable, failover routing to secondary region with warning banners and metric tags.
Each mode must be opt-in per route and have a reconciliation policy to rehydrate caches and drain buffers post-recovery.
acceptance_criteria: Dep-proxy unit tests for circuit-breaker transitions (closed -> open -> half-open -> closed)
Integration test: Redis read degraded path returns cached value with X-Dep-Proxy-Degraded header
Load test: under synthetic Redis overload, no node-level FD exhaustion and 90% fewer tail SLO violations versus baseline
Chaos test: simulate region outage and validate cross-region read fallback and write buffering behavior
Observability: per-tenant metrics, tracing (span tags), and alerts wired to PagerDuty for >5% error-rate over 1m

risks_and_tradeoffs:
Major tradeoffs:
- Returning stale reads reduces correctness for a class of requests. We mitigate by requiring opt-in per route and by surfacing staleness headers.
- Local durability for write buffers increases disk usage and recovery complexity after crash. Chosen because synchronous global write paths are more dangerous during outages.
- Cross-region fallbacks increase egress costs and latency; only used for low-consistency routes.
- Adding a proxy adds complexity and an additional failure surface; we minimize this by keeping it lightweight, stateless for most flows, and instrumented.
testing_plan:
Unit, integration, load and chaos tests. Staging scenario matrix:
- Redis overloaded (connections saturated): validate FD caps and queueing behavior.
- DB failover to standby: validate read-replica fallback and eventual reconciliation.
- Kafka broker partitioned: validate local buffering for publishes and replay to broker after heal.
Test artifacts and CI jobs: https://ci.redwood.ai/job/dep-proxy/
rollout_plan:
Phased rollout across regions:
1) Canary: 5% traffic from internal tenants in us-west-2 for 48h with detailed telemetry.
2) Expand to 25% after 72h if no regressions.
3) Full region rollout with 1h circuit monitoring windows.
Feature flags to control per-route opt-in and per-tenant defaults.
Rollback: feature flag off and drain local queues by replaying to upstream or dropping with compensating operation.
open_questions: What tenant-level defaults should we use for soft quotas vs hard caps? (SRE to propose tiered defaults)
Should the proxy support protocol-level pluggable adapters or stick with a narrow set (Redis, Postgres, Kafka)?
Recovery semantics: who is responsible for deduplication on replayed buffered writes? (application vs proxy)
